Before Halcyon shares patient data with a vendor, it needs a **signed business associate agreement (BAA)**. Halcyon's documents use "BAA" rather than "DPA," so the BAA is the contract that counts here. The knowledge base doesn't contain a standalone vendor-onboarding checklist, so the requirements below come from individual policies and vendor records.

**Core requirements**

- **Signed BAA first.** Under the HIPAA privacy policy, a vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate, and a signed BAA must exist before any PHI is disclosed. This applies to test files and pilots too, not just production data [1].
- **Security risk assessment.** The Tallgrass Survey record shows a security risk assessment completed before contracting, which passed with conditions [1]. The AI tools policy also requires one for any tool that will handle PHI [2].
- **Entry in the systems inventory.** Any system that holds PHI must be on the clinical and business systems inventory, which is the approved list under the HIPAA policy [6]. PHI may only be stored in approved systems [7].

The AI tools policy gives the most complete list for PHI-handling tools: a security risk assessment, a signed BAA, an inventory entry, and, for clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [2]. Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [2].

**Example from the knowledge base**

- Quillon Ambient (AI scribe) has an executed BAA dated July 30, 2026, and a completed security risk assessment from July 2026. The BAA prohibits training models on Halcyon data [4].
- Tallgrass Survey Co. has a completed security risk assessment but no executed BAA. Its order form is on hold, and no PHI can be shared until the BAA is signed. The open issue is data retention: Tallgrass wants 5 years, and Halcyon will accept 18 months [1].

Your question was about sharing data with a vendor in general. If your vendor will handle PHI, these are the requirements. If it won't, the policies above may not apply, but I'd confirm that with the Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway [2].

Northwind has a close equivalent, but it covers something different. Its emergency access is for engineers looking inside customer workspaces, not for patient records. Northwind doesn't handle EHR data, so the two processes aren't directly comparable.

**Northwind: emergency access to customer workspaces**
- **Trigger:** An open support case or a declared incident. "Curiosity" and "it would be faster" are not reasons [2].
- **Approval:** Requires a second engineer from support or on-call to approve in Teleport before access is granted. The approver can't be on the same case [2].
- **Scope:** Read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case first [2].
- **Duration:** Expires after 2 hours, shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [2][1].
- **Oversight:** Sessions are recorded and kept for one year. The customer's audit log shows that Northwind support accessed the workspace, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours. Security samples sessions each week, and reviews every session that used write access [2].

**Halcyon: break-the-glass in Meridian EHR**
- **Trigger:** Caring for a patient outside your normal panel, such as an unscheduled walk-in, covering a colleague's patient, or escalating a telehealth patient. It is never appropriate for family, coworkers, public figures, or yourself [8].
- **Approval:** None in the moment. You pick a reason (Emergency care, Coverage, or Other), type a justification, and get access. Your manager is asked to confirm the reason only if it isn't clear [8].
- **Duration:** Lasts until the end of your shift, up to 12 hours [8].
- **Oversight:** Every event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. Compliance also reviews EHR access logs monthly with automated anomaly detection [8][9]. Misuse is a privacy incident and can lead to termination [8].

**Main differences**
- **Who approves:** Northwind requires a second person before access starts. Halcyon grants access immediately and reviews afterward, because patient care comes first [2][8].
- **Access length:** Northwind's is 2 hours. Halcyon's can run up to 12 hours [2][8].
- **Default permissions:** Northwind is read-only unless the customer consents to writes. Halcyon's break-the-glass gives full chart access, bounded by the minimum-necessary rule [2][8].
- **Customer notice:** Northwind tells the customer when support enters their workspace. Halcyon's documents don't describe a patient notification step [2][8].

**Short answer: no, not for the most sensitive data at either company.** The rules differ in scope, though.

**Northwind Labs:** Restricted data never goes in Slack. That covers customer event payloads, credentials, and encryption keys, which "never leave production; never in tickets or Slack" [1]. When troubleshooting customer workspaces, use field names and counts instead of pasting payloads into Slack [3]. Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared on a need-to-know basis [1]. The policy doesn't explicitly ban Slack for that tier, so check with the data owner before sharing it there.

**Halcyon Health:** Slack is never an approved place for PHI, including DMs [2]. The inventory lists Slack under systems that must not hold PHI. For PHI in email, use `[secure]` encrypted email and keep PHI out of the subject line [2]. The sources I found don't cover non-PHI sensitive data in Slack, so I can't say more about that.

If sensitive data does end up in the wrong place at Northwind, report it right away in `#security-help`. You won't be penalized for reporting in good faith [1]. Halcyon's sources don't include an equivalent reporting channel, so I can't name one.

At Halcyon, a patient safety event goes into **SafeReport**. Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files the report, and reporting is never optional or punished [1].

**Who does what:**
- **Immediately:** Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed [1].
- **Charge nurse:** Tell the charge nurse on shift. In clinics without one, tell the clinic manager. The charge nurse coordinates the response [1].
- **Sentinel events (Level 1):** The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1].
- **Disclosure:** The attending clinician tells the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].

**Timing:** The policy section is headed "Within 24 hours," but the text I found doesn't state a specific filing deadline for SafeReport, so confirm that with Quality & Patient Safety [1]. Root cause analyses are charted within 72 hours and completed within 45 calendar days for Level 1 and 2 events [1].

**Related:** If the issue is a privacy incident, such as a misdirected fax or a lost device, report it to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [2]. Critical lab results have their own 60-minute escalation rule, and each notification is documented in the chart [5].

I didn't look up the Northwind `/incident declare` process, so I can't confirm how it compares.

Northwind Labs does run periodic access reviews, and access that nobody confirms is revoked automatically. I did not find an equivalent recertification process in the Halcyon Health documents.

**Northwind Labs**
- Quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead [3].
- Access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [3].
- Production access is granted through Teleport and expires after 8 hours, and standing production database access is not allowed [3].
- Exceptions need written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [3].

**Halcyon Health**
- The compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection. Unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [1].
- Access to clinical systems is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [1].
- Break-the-glass events are reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days [2].
- I did not find a documented process for periodically confirming that users still need their EHR (Meridian) access, or a rule for what happens if no one signs off. The knowledge base may hold this elsewhere, so it's worth checking with the Privacy Officer or the HIPAA Security Officer.

Northwind's EHR-related controls don't apply to Halcyon's Meridian EHR, which is a Halcyon system [5].

Halcyon requires four things before staff can use a new AI tool that handles PHI, and the usual turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly spent waiting on the business associate agreement (BAA) [8].

**Halcyon requirements** (email the Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway, and the HIPAA Security Officer, Ahmed Siddiqui) [8]:
1. A security risk assessment [8].
2. A signed business associate agreement with the vendor [8].
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory [8].
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [8].

Halcyon's policy also says PHI must never go into AI tools that are not on its approved list [8]. "De-identified" data still counts as PHI, since removing a name is not enough [8].

**Northwind's side:** Your question mentions Northwind's #vendor-review, and the knowledge base confirms that anything that will process customer data must clear that review before use [1]. However, I didn't find a documented steps list or typical timeline for #vendor-review in the sources. Northwind's vendor register does show that past reviews were logged as #vendor-review tickets, such as VR-88 for Cobaltline and VR-41 for Parcelwise [3][4]. Ask the Security team for their expected turnaround.

**Short answer:** At Halcyon, the equivalent is the **system steward** for the owning team. For a purely cosmetic change to the bill-pay screen, that steward's approval is enough on its own.

- **Who:** The Halcyon app is owned by Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), whose system steward is Felix Brandt [6][1].
- **Why it's enough:** Cosmetic changes are classed as minor, and minor changes need steward approval only [1].
- **What would change that:** Anything that touches patient-facing automation, the app's clinical content, medication information, orders or results routing needs more. That means a clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO (Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate Dr. Benedict Osei) and review at the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) [1]. Bill pay isn't in those categories, but a change that goes beyond appearance would need to be re-classed.

Halcyon's policy doesn't name a delegate for system stewards, unlike Northwind's change approvers. Check with Felix Brandt's team if he's unavailable.
